blocks.text: 8.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already studied about triangles, and in particular, right triangles, in your
earlier classes. Let us take some examples from our surroundings where right triangles
can be imagined to be formed. For instance :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. Suppose the students of a school are
visiting Qutub Minar. Now, if a student
is looking at the top of the Minar, a right
triangle can be imagined to be made,
as shown in Fig 8.1. Can the student
find out the height of the Minar, without
actually measuring it?

2. Suppose a girl is sitting on the balcony
of her house located on the bank of a
river. She is looking down at a flower
pot placed on a stair of a temple situated
nearby on the other bank of the river.
A right triangle is imagined to be made
in this situation as shown in Fig.8.2. If
you know the height at which the
person is sitting, can you find the width
of the river?

blocks.text: Fig. 8.1

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.2

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
3. Suppose a hot air balloon is flying in
the air. A girl happens to spot the
balloon in the sky and runs to her
mother to tell her about it. Her mother
rushes out of the house to look at the
balloon.Now when the girl had spotted

When both the mother and daughter

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In all the situations given above, the distances or heights can be found by using
some mathematical techniques, which come under a branch of mathematics called
‘trigonometry’. The word ‘trigonometry’ is derived from the Greek words ‘tri’
(meaning three), ‘gon’ (meaning sides) and ‘metron’ (meaning measure). In fact,
**trigonometry** is the study of relationships between the sides and angles of a triangle.
The earliest known work on trigonometry was recorded in Egypt and Babylon. Early
astronomers used it to find out the distances of the stars and planets from the Earth.
Even today, most of the technologically advanced methods used in Engineering and
Physical Sciences are based on trigonometrical concepts.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, we will study some ratios of the sides of a right triangle with
respect to its acute angles, called **trigonometric ratios of the angle**. We will restrict
our discussion to acute angles only. However, these ratios can be extended to other
angles also. We will also define the trigonometric ratios for angles of measure $0^{\circ}$ and
$90^{\circ}$. We will calculate trigonometric ratios for some specific angles and establish
some identities involving these ratios, called **trigonometric identities**.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.2 Trigonometric Ratios

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Section 8.1, you have seen some right triangles
imagined to be formed in different situations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us take a right triangle ABC as shown
in Fig. 8.4.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, $\angle$ CAB (or, in brief, angle A) is an
acute angle. Note the position of the side BC
with respect to angle A. It faces $\angle$ A. We call it
the \textit{side opposite} to angle A. AC is the
\textit{hypotenuse} of the right triangle and the side AB
is a part of $\angle$ A. So, we call it the \textit{side}
\textit{adjacent} to angle A.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.4

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that the position of sides change
when you consider angle C in place of A
(see Fig. 8.5).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have studied the concept of ‘ratio’ in
your earlier classes. We now define certain ratios
involving the sides of a right triangle, and call
them trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.5

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The trigonometric ratios of the angle A
in right triangle ABC (see Fig. 8.4) are defined
as follows :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{sine of } \angle A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{cosine of } \angle A = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$tangent \ of \angle A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} = \frac{BC}{AB}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{cosecant of } \angle A = \frac{1}{\text{sine of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{side opposite to angle A}} = \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{BC}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$secant \text{ of } \angle A = \frac{1}{\text{cosine of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} = \frac{AC}{AB}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{cotangent of } \angle A = \frac{1}{\text{tangent of } \angle A} = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{side opposite to angle A}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{BC}}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The ratios defined above are abbreviated as $\sin A$, $\cos A$, $\tan A$, $\text{cosec A}$, $\sec A$
and $\cot A$ respectively. Note that the ratios $\mathbf{cosec A}$, $\mathbf{sec A}$ and $\mathbf{cot A}$ are respectively,
the reciprocals of the ratios $\sin A$, $\cos A$ and $\tan A$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, observe that $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{\frac{BC}{AC}}{\frac{AB}{AC}} = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A}$ and $\cot A = \frac{\cos A}{\sin A}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the **trigonometric ratios** of an acute angle in a right triangle express the
relationship between the angle and the length of its sides.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Why don't you try to define the trigonometric ratios for angle C in the right
triangle? (See Fig. 8.5)

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
The first use of the idea of ‘**sine**’ in the way we use it today was in the work Aryabhatiyam by Aryabhata, in A.D. 500. Aryabhata used the word ardha-jya for the half-chord, which was shortened to jya or jiva in due course. When the Aryabhatiyam was translated into Arabic, the word jiva was retained as it is. The word jiva was translated into sinus, which means curve, when the Arabic version was translated into Latin. Soon the word sinus, also used as sine, became common in mathematical texts throughout Europe. An English Professor of astronomy Edmund Gunter (1581–1626), first used the abbreviated notation ‘**sin**’.

The origin of the terms ‘**cosine**’ and ‘**tangent**’ was much later. The cosine function arose from the need to compute the sine of the complementary angle. Aryabhatta called it **kotijya**. The name **cosinus** originated with Edmund Gunter. In 1674, the English Mathematician Sir Jonas Moore first used the abbreviated notation ‘**cos**’.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : Note that the symbol $\sin A$ is used as an
abbreviation for ‘the sine of the angle A’. $\sin A$ is $not$
the product of ‘$\sin$’ and A. ‘$\sin$’ separated from A
has no meaning. Similarly, $\cos A$ is $not$ the product of
‘$\cos$’ and A. Similar interpretations follow for other
trigonometric ratios also.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.6

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, if we take a point P on the hypotenuse
AC or a point Q on AC extended, of the right triangle
ABC and draw PM perpendicular to AB and QN
perpendicular to AB extended (see Fig. 8.6), how
will the trigonometric ratios of $\angle A$ in $\Delta$ PAM differ
from those of $\angle A$ in $\Delta$ CAB or from those of $\angle A$ in
$\Delta$ QAN?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To answer this, first look at these triangles. Is $\Delta$ PAM similar to $\Delta$ CAB? From
Chapter 6, recall the AA similarity criterion. Using the criterion, you will see that the
triangles PAM and CAB are similar. Therefore, by the property of similar triangles,
the corresponding sides of the triangles are proportional.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, we have $\frac{\text{AM}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{\text{AP}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{\text{MP}}{\text{BC}}.$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: From this, we find $$\frac{\mathrm{MP}}{\mathrm{AP}} = \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AC}} = \sin \mathrm{A}.$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly, $\frac{\mathrm{AM}}{\mathrm{AP}}=\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{AC}}=\cos \mathrm{A}, \frac{\mathrm{MP}}{\mathrm{AM}}=\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AB}}=\tan \mathrm{A}$ and so on.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This shows that the trigonometric ratios of angle A in $\Delta$ PAM not differ from
those of angle A in $\Delta$ CAB.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the same way, you should check that the value of $\sin A$ (and also of other
trigonometric ratios) remains the same in $\Delta QAN$ also.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From our observations, it is now clear that the values of the trigonometric
ratios of an angle do not vary with the lengths of the sides of the triangle, if
the angle remains the same.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Note :** For the sake of convenience, we may write $\sin^2\text{A}$, $\cos^2\text{A}$, etc., in place of
$(\sin \text{A})^2$, $(\cos \text{A})^2$, etc., respectively. But $\text{cosec A} = (\sin \text{A})^{-1} \neq \sin^{-1} \text{A}$ (it is called sine
inverse A). $\sin^{-1} \text{A}$ has a different meaning, which will be discussed in higher classes.
Similar conventions hold for the other trigonometric ratios as well. Sometimes, the
Greek letter $\theta$ (theta) is also used to denote an angle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have defined six trigonometric ratios of an acute angle. If we know any one
of the ratios, can we obtain the other ratios? Let us see.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If in a right triangle ABC, $\sin A = \frac{1}{3}$,
then this means that $\frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{1}{3}$, i.e., the
lengths of the sides BC and AC of the triangle
ABC are in the ratio $1:3$ (see Fig. 8.7). So if
BC is equal to $k$, then AC will be $3k$, where
$k$ is any positive number. To determine other
trigonometric ratios for the angle A, we need to find the length of the third side
AB. Do you remember the Pythagoras theorem? Let us use it to determine the
required length AB.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{Therefore, } \quad \text{AB}^2 = \text{AC}^2 - \text{BC}^2 = (3k)^2 - (k)^2 = 8k^2 = (2\sqrt{2}k)^2$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, we get $AB = 2\sqrt{2}k$ (Why is AB not $-2\sqrt{2}k$?)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}k}{3k} = \frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Similarly, you can obtain the other trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : Since the hypotenuse is the longest side in a right triangle, the value of
$\sin A$ or $\cos A$ is always less than 1 (or, in particular, equal to 1).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Given $\tan A = \frac{4}{3}$, find the other
trigonometric ratios of the angle A.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Let us first draw a right $\Delta$ ABC
(see Fig 8.8).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.8

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, we know that $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{4}{3}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Therefore, if BC $= 4k$, then AB $= 3k$, where $k$ is a
positive number.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, by using the Pythagoras Theorem, we have

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, we can write all the trigonometric ratios using their definitions.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{4k}{5k} = \frac{4}{5}$$
$$\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{3k}{5k} = \frac{3}{5}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\cot A = \frac{1}{\tan A} = \frac{3}{4}$, $\csc A = \frac{1}{\sin A} = \frac{5}{4}$ and $\sec A = \frac{1}{\cos A} = \frac{5}{3}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : If $\angle \text{ B}$ and $\angle \text{ Q}$ are
acute angles such that $\sin \text{ B} = \sin \text{ Q}$,
then prove that $\angle \text{ B} = \angle \text{ Q}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : Let us consider two right
triangles ABC and PQR where
$\sin B = \sin Q$ (see Fig. 8.9).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 8.9

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
We have $\sin \mathrm{B}=\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AB}}$
and $\sin \mathrm{Q}=\frac{\mathrm{PR}}{\mathrm{PQ}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then $\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AB}} = \frac{\mathrm{PR}}{\mathrm{PQ}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{PR}}=\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{PQ}}=k$, say (1)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, using Pythagoras theorem,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathrm{BC} = \sqrt{\mathrm{AB}^2 - \mathrm{AC}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and $QR = \sqrt{PQ^2 - PR^2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}} = \frac{\sqrt{\text{AB}^2 - \text{AC}^2}}{\sqrt{\text{PQ}^2 - \text{PR}^2}} = \frac{\sqrt{k^2\text{PQ}^2 - k^2\text{PR}^2}}{\sqrt{\text{PQ}^2 - \text{PR}^2}} = \frac{k\sqrt{\text{PQ}^2 - \text{PR}^2}}{\sqrt{\text{PQ}^2 - \text{PR}^2}} = k$ (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: From (1) and (2), we have

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\text{AC}}{\text{PR}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{PQ}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{QR}} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then, by using Theorem 6.4, $\Delta$ ACB $\sim \Delta$ PRQ and therefore, $\angle \mathrm{B} = \angle \mathrm{Q}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 3 : Consider $\Delta$ ACB, right-angled at C, in
which AB = 29 units, BC = 21 units and $\angle$ ABC = $\theta$
(see Fig. 8.10). Determine the values of
(i) $\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta$,
(ii) $\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta$.
Solution : In $\Delta$ ACB, we have
$$AC = \sqrt{AB^2 - BC^2} = \sqrt{(29)^2 - (21)^2}$$
$$= \sqrt{(29 - 21)(29 + 21)} = \sqrt{(8)(50)} = \sqrt{400} = 20 \text{units}$$
So, $\sin \theta = \frac{AC}{AB} = \frac{20}{29}$, $\cos \theta = \frac{BC}{AB} = \frac{21}{29}$.
Now, (i) $\cos^2 \theta + \sin^2 \theta = \left(\frac{20}{29}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{21}{29}\right)^2 = \frac{20^2 + 21^2}{29^2} = \frac{400 + 441}{841} = 1$,
and (ii) $\cos^2 \theta - \sin^2 \theta = \left(\frac{21}{29}\right)^2 - \left(\frac{20}{29}\right)^2 = \frac{(21 + 20)(21 - 20)}{29^2} = \frac{41}{841}$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B,
if $\tan A = 1$, then verify that
$2 \sin A \cos A = 1$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Solution : In $\Delta$ ABC, $\tan A = \frac{BC}{AB} = 1$ (see Fig 8.11)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e.,                                                                    $BC = AB$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let AB = BC = $k$, where $k$ is a positive number.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, $\text{AC} = \sqrt{\text{AB}^2 + \text{BC}^2}$

$= \sqrt{(k)^2 + (k)^2} = k\sqrt{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $2 \sin A \cos A = 2 \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) \left( \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = 1$, which is the required value.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5 : In $\Delta$ OPQ, right-angled at P,
OP = 7 cm and OQ – PQ = 1 cm (see Fig. 8.12).
Determine the values of $\sin$ Q and $\cos$ Q.

Solution : In $\Delta$ OPQ, we have

$$OQ^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2$$

i.e., $$(1 + PQ)^2 = OP^2 + PQ^2 \quad \text{(Why?)}$$

i.e., $1 + PQ^2 + 2PQ = OP^2 + PQ^2$

i.e., $1 + 2PQ = 7^2 \quad \text{(Why?)}$

i.e., $PQ = 24 \text{ cm and } OQ = 1 + PQ = 25 \text{ cm}$

So, $\sin Q = \frac{7}{25}$ and $\cos Q = \frac{24}{25}$.

blocks.text: 8.3 Trigonometric Ratios of Some Specific Angles

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From geometry, you are already familiar with the construction of angles of $30^{\circ}$, $45^{\circ}$,
$60^{\circ}$ and $90^{\circ}$. In this section, we will find the values of the trigonometric ratios for these
angles and, of course, for $0^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $45^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B, if one angle is $45^{\circ}$, then
the other angle is also $45^{\circ}$, i.e., $\angle A = \angle C = 45^{\circ}$
(see Fig. 8.14).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\text{BC} = \text{AB} \quad (\text{Why?})$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, Suppose BC = AB = $a$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Then by Pythagoras Theorem, $\mathrm{AC}^2 = \mathrm{AB}^2 + \mathrm{BC}^2 = a^2 + a^2 = 2a^2$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: and, therefore, $\text{AC} = a\sqrt{2}.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using the definitions of the trigonometric ratios, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \sin 45^{\circ} = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle } 45^{\circ}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\cos 45^{\circ} = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle } 45^{\circ}}{\text{hypotenuse}} = \frac{\text{AB}}{\text{AC}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \tan 45^{\circ} = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle } 45^{\circ}}{\text{side adjacent to angle } 45^{\circ}} = \frac{\text{BC}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a}{a} = 1 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, $\csc 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 45^{\circ}} = \sqrt{2}$, $\sec 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\cos 45^{\circ}} = \sqrt{2}$, $\cot 45^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\tan 45^{\circ}} = 1$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us now calculate the trigonometric ratios of $30^{\circ}$
and $60^{\circ}$. Consider an equilateral triangle ABC. Since
each angle in an equilateral triangle is $60^{\circ}$, therefore,
$\angle A = \angle B = \angle C = 60^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Draw the perpendicular AD from A to the side BC
(see Fig. 8.15).

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now $\Delta \mathrm{ABD} \cong \Delta \mathrm{ACD}$ (Why?)
Therefore, $\mathrm{BD}=\mathrm{DC}$
and $\angle \mathrm{BAD}=\angle \mathrm{CAD}$ (CPCT)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now observe that:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\Delta$ ABD is a right triangle, right-angled at D with $\angle$ BAD $= 30^{\circ}$ and $\angle$ ABD $= 60^{\circ}$
(see Fig. 8.15).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As you know, for finding the trigonometric ratios, we need to know the lengths of the
sides of the triangle. So, let us suppose that $\text{AB} = 2a$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Then, $\text{BD} = \frac{1}{2}\text{BC} = a$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AD = a\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
ve :
$\sin 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a}{2a} = \frac{1}{2}, \cos 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2a} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$
$\tan 30^{\circ} = \frac{\text{BD}}{\text{AD}} = \frac{a}{a\sqrt{3}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Also, $\quad \operatorname{cosec} 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\sin 30^{\circ}}=2, \quad \sec 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\cos 30^{\circ}}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$
$\cot 30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{\tan 30^{\circ}}=\sqrt{3}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Similarly,
$$\sin 60^{\circ} = \frac{\text{AD}}{\text{AB}} = \frac{a\sqrt{3}}{2a} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}, \cos 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{2}, \tan 60^{\circ} = \sqrt{3},$$
$$\text{cosec } 60^{\circ} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}, \sec 60^{\circ} = 2 \text{ and } \cot 60^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}.$$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Trigonometric Ratios of $0^\circ$ and $90^\circ$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see what happens to the trigonometric ratios of angle
A, if it is made smaller and smaller in the right triangle ABC
(see Fig. 8.16), till it becomes zero. As $\angle$ A gets smaller and
smaller, the length of the side BC decreases.The point C gets
closer to point B, and finally when $\angle$ A becomes very close
to $0^{\circ}$, AC becomes almost the same as AB (see Fig. 8.17).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When $\angle A$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, BC gets very close to $0$ and so the value of
$\sin A = \frac{BC}{AC}$ is very close to $0$. Also, when $\angle A$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, AC is nearly the

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: same as AB and so the value of $\cos A = \frac{AB}{AC}$ is very close to 1.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This helps us to see how we can define the values of $\sin A$ and $\cos A$ when
$A = 0^\circ$. We define : $\mathbf{sin}\ \mathbf{0}^\circ = \mathbf{0}$ and $\mathbf{cos}\ \mathbf{0}^\circ = \mathbf{1}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using these, we have :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\tan 0^{\circ} = \frac{\sin 0^{\circ}}{\cos 0^{\circ}} = 0, \cot 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\tan 0^{\circ}}, \text{ which is not defined. (Why?)}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\sec 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\cos 0^{\circ}} = 1$ and $\csc 0^{\circ} = \frac{1}{\sin 0^{\circ}}$, which is again not defined.(Why?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us see what happens to the trigonometric ratios of $\angle A$, when it is made
larger and larger in $\Delta ABC$ till it becomes $90^\circ$. As $\angle A$ gets larger and larger, $\angle C$ gets
smaller and smaller. Therefore, as in the case above, the length of the side AB goes on
decreasing. The point A gets closer to point B. Finally when $\angle A$ is very close to $90^\circ$,
$\angle C$ becomes very close to $0^\circ$ and the side AC almost coincides with side BC
(see Fig. 8.18).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When $\angle C$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, $\angle A$ is very close to $90^{\circ}$, side AC is nearly the
same as side BC, and so $\sin A$ is very close to $1$. Also when $\angle A$ is very close to $90^{\circ}$,
$\angle C$ is very close to $0^{\circ}$, and the side AB is nearly zero, so $\cos A$ is very close to $0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we define : $\sin 90^\circ = 1$ and $\cos 90^\circ = 0$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, why don’t you find the other trigonometric ratios of $90^\circ$?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We shall now give the values of all the trigonometric ratios of $0^{\circ}$, $30^{\circ}$, $45^{\circ}$, $60^{\circ}$
and $90^{\circ}$ in Table 8.1, for ready reference.

$\tan A$ 0 $\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$ 1 $\sqrt{3}$ Not defined

**Remark :** From the table above you can observe that as $\angle$ A increases from $0^\circ$ to

Example 6 : In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B,
AB = 5 cm and $\angle$ ACB = $30^\circ$ (see Fig. 8.19).

$$\frac{\text{AB}}{\text{BC}} = \tan \text{C}$$

i.e., $$\frac{5}{\text{BC}} = \tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}$$

Note that alternatively we could have used Pythagoras theorem to determine the third

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.4 Trigonometric Identities

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may recall that an equation is called an identity
when it is true for all values of the variables involved.
Similarly, an equation involving trigonometric ratios
of an angle is called a **trigonometric identity**, if it is
true for all values of the angle(s) involved.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this section, we will prove one trigonometric
identity, and use it further to prove other useful
trigonometric identities.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In $\Delta$ ABC, right-angled at B (see Fig. 8.21), we have:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Dividing each term of (1) by $AC^2$, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}^2}{\mathrm{AC}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\left(\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{AC}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AC}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AC}}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\cos^2 \mathrm{A} + \sin^2 \mathrm{A} = 1$ (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This is true for all A such that $0^{\circ} \leq A \leq 90^{\circ}$. So, this is a trigonometric identity.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us now divide (1) by $AB^2$. We get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{AB}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{AB}^2} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}^2}{\mathrm{AB}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or, $\left(\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{AB}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{AB}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AB}}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Is this equation true for $A = 0^{\circ}$? Yes, it is. What about $A = 90^{\circ}$? Well, $\tan A$ and
sec A are not defined for $A = 90^{\circ}$. So, (3) is true for all A such that $0^{\circ} \le A < 90^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us see what we get on dividing (1) by $\text{BC}^2$. We get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\mathrm{AB}^2}{\mathrm{BC}^2} + \frac{\mathrm{BC}^2}{\mathrm{BC}^2} = \frac{\mathrm{AC}^2}{\mathrm{BC}^2} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\left(\frac{\mathrm{AB}}{\mathrm{BC}}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\mathrm{BC}}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{BC}}\right)^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\cot^2 \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{1} = \operatorname{cosec}^2 \mathbf{A}$ (4)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that cosec A and cot A are not defined for $A = 0^{\circ}$. Therefore (4) is true for
all A such that $0^{\circ} < A \leq 90^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Using these identities, we can express each trigonometric ratio in terms of other
trigonometric ratios, i.e., if any one of the ratios is known, we can also determine the
values of other trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see how we can do this using these identities. Suppose we know that

$$\tan A = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \text{ . Then, } \cot A = \sqrt{3} \text{ .}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Since, $\sec^2 A = 1 + \tan^2 A = 1 + \frac{1}{3} = \frac{4}{3}$, $\sec A = \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}$, and $\cos A = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Again, $\sin A = \sqrt{1 - \cos^2 A} = \sqrt{1 - \frac{3}{4}} = \frac{1}{2}$. Therefore, $\csc A = 2$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 9 : Express the ratios $\cos A$, $\tan A$ and $\sec A$ in terms of $\sin A$.

Solution : Since $\cos^2 A + \sin^2 A = 1$, therefore,

$$\cos^2 A = 1 - \sin^2 A, \text{ i.e., } \cos A = \pm \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}$$

This gives $\cos A = \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A} \quad (\text{Why?})$

Hence, $\tan A = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A} = \frac{\sin A}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}}$ and $\sec A = \frac{1}{\cos A} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^2 A}}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 10 : Prove that $\sec A (1 - \sin A)(\sec A + \tan A) = 1$.
Solution :

$$LHS = \sec A (1 - \sin A)(\sec A + \tan A) = \left( \frac{1}{\cos A} \right) (1 - \sin A) \left( \frac{1}{\cos A} + \frac{\sin A}{\cos A} \right)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ = \frac{(1 - \sin A)(1 + \sin A)}{\cos^2 A} = \frac{1 - \sin^2 A}{\cos^2 A} $$

$$ = \frac{\cos^2 A}{\cos^2 A} = 1 = \text{RHS} $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Example 11 : Prove that $\frac{\cot A - \cos A}{\cot A + \cos A} = \frac{\text{cosec } A - 1}{\text{cosec } A + 1}$

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution : $\text{LHS} = \frac{\cot A - \cos A}{\cot A + \cos A} = \frac{\frac{\cos A}{\sin A} - \cos A}{\frac{\cos A}{\sin A} + \cos A}$
$= \frac{\cos A \left( \frac{1}{\sin A} - 1 \right)}{\cos A \left( \frac{1}{\sin A} + 1 \right)} = \frac{\left( \frac{1}{\sin A} - 1 \right)}{\left( \frac{1}{\sin A} + 1 \right)} = \frac{\text{cosec A} - 1}{\text{cosec A} + 1} = \text{RHS}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 12 : Prove that $\frac{\sin \theta - \cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta - 1} = \frac{1}{\sec \theta - \tan \theta}$, using the identity
$\sec^2 \theta = 1 + \tan^2 \theta$.

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Solution : Since we will apply the identity involving $\sec \theta$ and $\tan \theta$, let us first
convert the LHS (of the identity we need to prove) in terms of $\sec \theta$ and $\tan \theta$ by
dividing numerator and denominator by $\cos \theta$.

$$LHS = \frac{\sin \theta - \cos \theta + 1}{\sin \theta + \cos \theta - 1} = \frac{\tan \theta - 1 + \sec \theta}{\tan \theta + 1 - \sec \theta}$$

$$= \frac{(\tan \theta + \sec \theta) - 1}{(\tan \theta - \sec \theta) + 1} = \frac{\{(\tan \theta + \sec \theta) - 1\} (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}{\{(\tan \theta - \sec \theta) + 1\} (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}$$

$$= \frac{(\tan^2 \theta - \sec^2 \theta) - (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}{\{\tan \theta - \sec \theta + 1\} (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}$$

$$= \frac{- 1 - \tan \theta + \sec \theta}{(\tan \theta - \sec \theta + 1) (\tan \theta - \sec \theta)}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{-1}{\tan \theta - \sec \theta} = \frac{1}{\sec \theta - \tan \theta}, $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: which is the RHS of the identity, we are required to prove.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 8.5 Summary

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. In a right triangle ABC, right-angled at B,
$$ \sin A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}}, \cos A = \frac{\text{side adjacent to angle A}}{\text{hypotenuse}} $$
$$ \tan A = \frac{\text{side opposite to angle A}}{\text{side adjacent to angle A}} . $$
2. $\text{cosec A} = \frac{1}{\sin A}; \text{sec A} = \frac{1}{\cos A}; \tan A = \frac{1}{\cot A}, \tan A = \frac{\sin A}{\cos A}$.
3. If one of the trigonometric ratios of an acute angle is known, the remaining trigonometric
ratios of the angle can be easily determined.
4. The values of trigonometric ratios for angles $0^\circ, 30^\circ, 45^\circ, 60^\circ$ and $90^\circ$.
5. The value of $\sin A$ or $\cos A$ never exceeds 1, whereas the value of $\sec A$ or $\text{cosec A}$ is
always greater than or equal to 1.
6. $\sin^2 A + \cos^2 A = 1$,
$\sec^2 A - \tan^2 A = 1$ for $0^\circ \le A < 90^\circ$,
$\text{cosec}^2 A = 1 + \cot^2 A$ for $0^\circ < A \le 90^\circ$.

blocks.text: 9.1 Heights and Distances

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous chapter, you have studied about trigonometric ratios. In this chapter,
you will be studying about some ways in which trigonometry is used in the life around
you.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider Fig. 8.1 of prvious chapter, which is redrawn below in Fig. 9.1.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this figure, the line AC drawn from the eye of the student to the top of the
minar is called the \textit{line of sight}. The student is looking at the top of the minar. The
angle BAC, so formed by the line of sight with the horizontal, is called the \textit{angle of}
\textit{elevation} of the top of the minar from the eye of the student.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, the **line of sight** is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point
in the object viewed by the observer. The **angle of elevation** of the point viewed is

blocks.label: Paragraph
Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.2

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, consider the situation given in Fig. 8.2. The girl sitting on the balcony is
looking down at a flower pot placed on a stair of the temple. In this case, the line of
sight is below the horizontal level. The angle so formed by the line of sight with the
horizontal is called the angle of depression.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, the **angle of depression** of a point on the object being viewed is the angle
formed by the line of sight with the horizontal when the point is below the horizontal
level, i.e., the case when we lower our head to look at the point being viewed
(see Fig. 9.3).

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 9.3

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, you may identify the lines of sight, and the angles so formed in Fig. 8.3.
Are they angles of elevation or angles of depression?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us refer to Fig. 9.1 again. If you want to find the height CD of the minar
without actually measuring it, what information do you need? You would need to know
the following:

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: (i) the distance DE at which the student is standing from the foot of the minar

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: SOME APPLICATIONS OF TRIGONOMETRY

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(ii) the angle of elevation, $\angle$ BAC, of the top of the minar
(iii) the height AE of the student.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Assuming that the above three conditions are known, how can we determine the
height of the minar?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the figure, CD = CB + BD. Here, BD = AE, which is the height of the student.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: To find BC, we will use trigonometric ratios of $\angle$ BAC or $\angle$ A.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In $\Delta$ ABC, the side BC is the opposite side in relation to the known $\angle$ A. Now,
which of the trigonometric ratios can we use? Which one of them has the two values
that we have and the one we need to determine? Our search narrows down to using

blocks.label: Equation

blocks.label: Paragraph

**Example 1 :** A tower stands vertically on the ground. From a point on the ground,
which is 15 m away from the foot of the tower, the angle of elevation of the top of the
tower is found to be $60^{\circ}$. Find the height of the tower.

**Solution :** First let us draw a simple diagram to
represent the problem (see Fig. 9.4). Here AB
represents the tower, CB is the distance of the point
from the tower and $\angle ACB$ is the angle of elevation.
We need to determine the height of the tower, i.e.,
AB. Also, ACB is a triangle, right-angled at B.

To solve the problem, we choose the trigonometric
ratio $\tan 60^{\circ}$ (or $\cot 60^{\circ}$), as the ratio involves AB
and BC.

Now, $\tan 60^{\circ} = \frac{AB}{BC}$

i.e., $\sqrt{3} = \frac{AB}{15}$

i.e., $AB = 15\sqrt{3}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the height of the tower is $15\sqrt{3}$ m.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In this chapter, you have studied the following points :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
**1. (i) The line of sight** is the line drawn from the eye of an observer to the point in the
object viewed by the observer.

(ii) The **angle of elevation** of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight
with the horizontal when it is above the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we raise
our head to look at the object.

(iii) The **angle of depression** of an object viewed, is the angle formed by the line of sight
with the horizontal when it is below the horizontal level, i.e., the case when we lower
our head to look at the object.

**2. The height or length of an object or the distance between two distant objects can be**
determined with the help of trigonometric ratios.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have studied in Class IX that a circle is a collection of all points in a plane
which are at a constant distance (radius) from a fixed point (centre). You have
also studied various terms related to a circle like chord, segment, sector, arc etc.
Let us now examine the different situations that can arise when a circle and a line
are given in a plane.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, let us consider a circle and a line PQ. There can be three possibilities given
in Fig. 10.1 below:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Fig. 10.1 (i), the line PQ and the circle have no common point. In this case,
PQ is called a **non-intersecting** line with respect to the circle. In Fig. 10.1 (ii), there
are two common points A and B that the line PQ and the circle have. In this case, we
call the line PQ a **secant** of the circle. In Fig. 10.1 (iii), there is only one point A which
is common to the line PQ and the circle. In this case, the line is called a **tangent** to the
circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You might have seen a pulley fitted over a well which is used
in taking out water from the well. Look at Fig. 10.2. Here the rope
on both sides of the pulley, if considered as a ray, is like a tangent
to the circle representing the pulley.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Is there any position of the line with respect to the circle
other than the types given above? You can see that there cannot
be any other type of position of the line with respect to the circle.
In this chapter, we will study about the existence of the tangents
to a circle and also study some of their properties.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 10.2 Tangent to a Circle

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous section, you have seen that **a tangent*** to a circle is a line that
intersects the circle at only one point.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To understand the existence of the tangent to a circle at a point, let us perform
the following activities:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 1 : Take a circular wire and attach a straight wire AB at a point P of the
circular wire so that it can rotate about the point P in a plane. Put the system on a table
and gently rotate the wire AB about the point P to get different positions of the straight
wire [see Fig. 10.3(i)].

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In various positions, the wire intersects the
circular wire at P and at another point $Q_1$ or $Q_2$ or
$Q_3$, etc. In one position, you will see that it will
intersect the circle at the point P only (see position
A'B' of AB). This shows that a tangent exists at
the point P of the circle. On rotating further, you
can observe that in all other positions of AB, it will
intersect the circle at P and at another point, say $R_1$
or $R_2$ or $R_3$, etc. So, you can observe that **there is**
**only one tangent at a point of the circle.**

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
While doing activity above, you must have observed that as the position AB
moves towards the position $A' B'$, the common point, say $Q_1$, of the line AB and the
circle gradually comes nearer and nearer to the common point P. Ultimately, it coincides
with the point P in the position $A'B'$ of $A''B''$. Again note, what happens if ‘AB’ is
rotated rightwards about P? The common point $R_3$ gradually comes nearer and nearer
to P and ultimately coincides with P. So, what we see is:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The tangent to a circle is a special case of the secant, when the two end
points of its corresponding chord coincide.

blocks.label: Footnote
blocks.text:
*The word ‘tangent’ comes from the Latin word ‘tangere’, which means to touch and was
introduced by the Danish mathematician Thomas Fineke in 1583.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 2 : On a paper, draw a circle and a
secant PQ of the circle. Draw various lines
parallel to the secant on both sides of it. You
will find that after some steps, the length of
the chord cut by the lines will gradually
decrease, i.e., the two points of intersection of
the line and the circle are coming closer and
closer [see Fig. 10.3(ii)]. In one case, it
becomes zero on one side of the secant and in
another case, it becomes zero on the other side
of the secant. See the positions $P'Q'$ and $P''Q''$
of the secant in Fig. 10.3 (ii). These are the
tangents to the circle parallel to the given secant
PQ. This also helps you to see that there cannot
be more than two tangents parallel to a given
secant.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: Fig. 10.3 (ii)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
This activity also establishes, what you must have observed, while doing
Activity 1, namely, a tangent is the secant when both of the end points of the
corresponding chord coincide.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The common point of the tangent and the circle is called the **point of contact**
[the point A in Fig. 10.1 (iii)]and the tangent is said to **touch** the circle at the
common point.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now look around you. Have you seen a bicycle
or a cart moving? Look at its wheels. All the spokes
of a wheel are along its radii. Now note the position
of the wheel with respect to its movement on the
ground. Do you see any tangent anywhere?
(See Fig. 10.4). In fact, the wheel moves along a line
which is a tangent to the circle representing the wheel.
Also, notice that in all positions, the radius through
the point of contact with the ground appears to be at
right angles to the tangent (see Fig. 10.4). We shall
now prove this property of the tangent.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Theorem 10.1 :** *The tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the*
*radius through the point of contact.*

**Proof :** We are given a circle with centre O and a tangent XY to the circle at a
point P. We need to prove that OP is perpendicular to XY.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: CIRCLES

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Take a point Q on XY other than P and join OQ (see Fig. 10.5).

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The point Q must lie outside the circle.
(Why? Note that if Q lies inside the circle, XY
will become a secant and not a tangent to the
circle). Therefore, OQ is longer than the radius
OP of the circle. That is,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $OQ > OP.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Since this happens for every point on the
line $XY$ except the point $P$, $OP$ is the
shortest of all the distances of the point $O$ to the
points of $XY$. So $OP$ is perpendicular to $XY$.
(as shown in Theorem A1.7.)

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. By theorem above, we can also conclude that at any point on a circle there can be
one and only one tangent.
2. The line containing the radius through the point of contact is also sometimes called
the ‘normal’ to the circle at the point.

blocks.text: 10.3 Number of Tangents from a Point on a Circle

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
To get an idea of the number of tangents from a point on a circle, let us perform the
following activity:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 3 : Draw a circle on a paper. Take a
point P inside it. Can you draw a tangent to the
circle through this point? You will find that all
the lines through this point intersect the circle in
two points. So, it is not possible to draw any
tangent to a circle through a point inside it
[see Fig. 10.6 (i)].

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Next take a point P on the circle and draw
tangents through this point. You have already
observed that there is only one tangent to the
circle at such a point [see Fig. 10.6 (ii)].

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Finally, take a point P outside the circle and
try to draw tangents to the circle from this point.
What do you observe? You will find that you
can draw exactly two tangents to the circle
through this point [see Fig. 10.6 (iii)].

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We can summarise these facts as follows:

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: (ii)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case 1 : There is no tangent to a circle passing
through a point lying inside the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case 2 : There is one and only one tangent to a
circle passing through a point lying on the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Case 3 : There are exactly two tangents to a
circle through a point lying outside the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Fig. 10.6 (iii), $\text{T}_1$ and $\text{T}_2$ are the points of
contact of the tangents $\text{PT}_1$ and $\text{PT}_2$
respectively.

blocks.label: Image-caption

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The length of the segment of the tangent
from the external point P and the point of contact
with the circle is called the **length of the tangent**
from the point P to the circle.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that in Fig. 10.6 (iii), $\text{PT}_1$ and $\text{PT}_2$ are the lengths of the tangents from P to
the circle. The lengths $\text{PT}_1$ and $\text{PT}_2$ have a common property. Can you find this?
Measure $\text{PT}_1$ and $\text{PT}_2$. Are these equal? In fact, this is always so. Let us give a proof
of this fact in the following theorem.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: CIRCLES

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Theorem 10.2 : The lengths of tangents drawn
from an external point to a circle are equal.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Proof : We are given a circle with centre O, a
point P lying outside the circle and two tangents
PQ, PR on the circle from P (see Fig. 10.7). We
are required to prove that PQ = PR.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For this, we join OP, OQ and OR. Then
$\angle$ OQP and $\angle$ ORP are right angles, because
these are angles between the radii and tangents,
and according to Theorem 10.1 they are right
angles. Now in right triangles OQP and ORP,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$OQ = OR \quad \text{(Radii of the same circle)}$$
$$OP = OP \quad \text{(Common)}$$
$$\Delta OQP \cong \Delta ORP \quad \text{(RHS)}$$
$$PQ = PR \quad \text{(CPCT)}$$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Remarks

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. The theorem can also be proved by using the Pythagoras Theorem as follows:
$$PQ^2 = OP^2 - OQ^2 = OP^2 - OR^2 = PR^2 \text{ (As } OQ = OR)$$
which gives $PQ = PR$.
2. Note also that $\angle OPQ = \angle OPR$. Therefore, OP is the angle bisector of $\angle QPR$,
i.e., the centre lies on the bisector of the angle between the two tangents.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 11.1 Areas of Sector and Segment of a Circle

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You have already come across the terms $sector$ and
$segment$ of a circle in your earlier classes. Recall
that the portion (or part) of the circular region enclosed
by two radii and the corresponding arc is called a
$sector$ of the circle and the portion (or part) of the
circular region enclosed between a chord and the
corresponding arc is called a $segment$ of the circle.
Thus, in Fig. 11.1, shaded region OAPB is a $sector$
of the circle with centre O. $\angle$ AOB is called the
$angle$ of the sector. Note that in this figure, unshaded region OAQB is also a sector of
the circle. For obvious reasons, OAPB is called the $minor$ $sector$ and
OAQB is called the $major$ $sector$. You can also see that angle of the major sector is
$360^\circ - \angle$ AOB.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, look at Fig. 11.2 in which AB is a chord
of the circle with centre O. So, shaded region APB is
a segment of the circle. You can also note that
unshaded region AQB is another segment of the circle
formed by the chord AB. For obvious reasons, APB
is called the $minor$ $segment$ and AQB is called the
$major$ $segment$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Remark : When we write ‘segment’ and ‘sector’
we will mean the ‘minor segment’ and the ‘minor
sector’ respectively, unless stated otherwise.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: AREAS RELATED TO CIRCLES

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now with this knowledge, let us try to find some
relations (or formulae) to calculate their areas.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let OAPB be a sector of a circle with centre
O and radius $r$ (see Fig. 11.3). Let the degree
measure of $\angle AOB$ be $\theta$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You know that area of a circle (in fact of a
circular region or disc) is $\pi r^2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In a way, we can consider this circular region to
be a sector forming an angle of $360^{\circ}$ (i.e., of degree
measure 360) at the centre O. Now by applying the
Unitary Method, we can arrive at the area of the
sector OAPB as follows:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When degree measure of the angle at the centre is 360, area of the
sector = $\pi r^2$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, when the degree measure of the angle at the centre is 1, area of the
sector = $\frac{\pi r^2}{360}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, when the degree measure of the angle at the centre is $\theta$, area of the

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{sector} = \frac{\pi r^2}{360} \times \theta = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2 . $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Thus, we obtain the following relation (or formula) for area of a sector of a
circle:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Area of the sector of angle $\theta = \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: where $r$ is the radius of the circle and $\theta$ the angle of the sector in degrees.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, a natural question arises : Can we find
the length of the arc APB corresponding to this
sector? Yes. Again, by applying the Unitary
Method and taking the whole length of the circle
(of angle $360^\circ$) as $2\pi r$, we can obtain the required
length of the arc APB as $\frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, length of an arc of a sector of angle $\theta = \frac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi r$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now let us take the case of the area of the
segment APB of a circle with centre O and radius $r$
(see Fig. 11.4). You can see that :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Area of the segment APB = Area of the sector OAPB – Area of $\Delta$ OAB
$$= \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2$ – area of $\Delta$ OAB

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: **Note :** From Fig. 11.3 and Fig. 11.4 respectively, you can observe that:

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Area of the major sector OAQB = $\pi r^2$ – Area of the minor sector OAPB
and Area of major segment AQB = $\pi r^2$ – Area of the minor segment APB
Let us now take some examples to understand these concepts (or results).

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Find the area of the sector of a circle
with radius 4 cm and of angle $30^{\circ}$. Also, find the area
of the corresponding major sector (Use $\pi = 3.14$).
Solution : Given sector is OAPB (see Fig. 11.5).

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Area of the sector} &= \frac{\theta}{360} \times \pi r^2 \\
&= \frac{30}{360} \times 3.14 \times 4 \times 4 \text{ cm}^2 \\
&= \frac{12.56}{3} \text{ cm}^2 = 4.19 \text{ cm}^2 \text{ (approx.)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Area of the corresponding major sector
$$
\begin{aligned}
&= \pi r^2 - \text{area of sector OAPB} \\
&= (3.14 \times 16 - 4.19) \text{ cm}^2 \\
&= 46.05 \text{ cm}^2 = 46.1 \text{ cm}^2 \text{ (approx.)}
\end{aligned}
$$

Alternatively, area of the major sector $= \frac{(360 - \theta)}{360} \times \pi r^2$
$$
= \left( \frac{360 - 30}{360} \right) \times 3.14 \times 16 \text{ cm}^2
$$
$$
= \frac{330}{360} \times 3.14 \times 16 \text{ cm}^2 = 46.05 \text{ cm}^2
$$
$$
= 46.1 \text{ cm}^2 \text{ (approx.)}
$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : Find the area of the segment AYB
shown in Fig. 11.6, if radius of the circle is 21 cm and
$\angle \text{AOB} = 120^{\circ}$. (Use $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ )

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Solution : Area of the segment AYB
$$= \text{Area of sector OAYB} - \text{Area of } \Delta \text{ OAB} \quad (1)$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Now, area of the sector OAYB = $\frac{120}{360} \times \frac{22}{7} \times 21 \times 21 \text{ cm}^2 = 462 \text{ cm}^2$ (2)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For finding the area of $\Delta$ OAB, draw OM $\perp$ AB as shown in Fig. 11.7.
Note that OA = OB. Therefore, by RHS congruence, $\Delta$ AMO $\cong \Delta$ BMO.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, M is the mid-point of AB and $\angle AOM = \angle BOM = \frac{1}{2} \times 120^\circ = 60^\circ$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Let $\text{OM} = x \text{ cm}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, from $\Delta$ OMA, $\frac{\text{OM}}{\text{OA}} = \cos 60^{\circ}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: or, $\frac{x}{21} = \frac{1}{2} \left( \cos 60^\circ = \frac{1}{2} \right)$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $$OM = \frac{21}{2} \text{ cm}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Also, $\frac{\text{AM}}{\text{OA}} = \sin 60^\circ = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $AM = \frac{21\sqrt{3}}{2}$ cm

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $AB = 2 AM = \frac{2 \times 21\sqrt{3}}{2} \text{ cm} = 21\sqrt{3} \text{ cm}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So, $\text{area of } \Delta \text{ OAB} = \frac{1}{2} \text{ AB } \times \text{ OM} = \frac{1}{2} \times 21\sqrt{3} \times \frac{21}{2} \text{ cm}^2$
$= \frac{441}{4} \sqrt{3} \text{ cm}^2$ (3)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Therefore, area of the segment AYB = $\left(462-\frac{441}{4}\sqrt{3}\right)\mathrm{cm}^2$ [From (1), (2) and (3)]
$$=\frac{21}{4}(88-21\sqrt{3})\mathrm{cm}^2$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 12.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
From Class IX, you are familiar with some of the solids like cuboid, cone, cylinder, and
sphere (see Fig. 12.1). You have also learnt how to find their surface areas and volumes.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In our day-to-day life, we come across a number of solids made up of combinations
of two or more of the basic solids as shown above.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You must have seen a truck with a
container fitted on its back (see Fig. 12.2),
carrying oil or water from one place to
another. Is it in the shape of any of the four
basic solids mentioned above? You may
guess that it is made of a cylinder with two
hemispheres as its ends.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Again, you may have seen an object like the
one in Fig. 12.3. Can you name it? A test tube, right!
You would have used one in your science laboratory.
This tube is also a combination of a cylinder and a
hemisphere. Similarly, while travelling, you may have
seen some big and beautiful buildings or monuments
made up of a combination of solids mentioned above.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If for some reason you wanted to find the
surface areas, or volumes, or capacities of such
objects, how would you do it? We cannot classify
these under any of the solids you have already studied.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In this chapter, you will see how to find surface areas and volumes of such
objects.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 12.2 Surface Area of a Combination of Solids

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us consider the container seen in Fig. 12.2. How do we find the surface area of
such a solid? Now, whenever we come across a new problem, we first try to see, if
we can break it down into smaller problems, we have earlier solved. We can see that
this solid is made up of a cylinder with two hemispheres stuck at either end. It would
look like what we have in Fig. 12.4, after we put the pieces all together.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If we consider the surface of the newly formed object, we would be able to see
only the curved surfaces of the two hemispheres and the curved surface of the cylinder.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the \textit{total} surface area of the new solid is the sum of the \textit{curved} surface
areas of each of the individual parts. This gives,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
TSA of new solid = CSA of one hemisphere + CSA of cylinder
+ CSA of other hemisphere

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
where TSA, CSA stand for ‘Total Surface Area’ and ‘Curved Surface Area’
respectively.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us now consider another situation. Suppose we are making a toy by putting
together a hemisphere and a cone. Let us see the steps that we would be going
through.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
First, we would take a cone and a hemisphere and bring their flat faces together.
Here, of course, we would take the base radius of the cone equal to the radius of the
hemisphere, for the toy is to have a smooth surface. So, the steps would be as shown
in Fig. 12.5.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
At the end of our trial, we have got ourselves a nice round-bottomed toy. Now if
we want to find how much paint we would require to colour the surface of this toy,
what would we need to know? We would need to know the surface area of the toy,
which consists of the CSA of the hemisphere and the CSA of the cone.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, we can say:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Total surface area of the toy = CSA of hemisphere + CSA of cone

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, let us consider some examples.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 1 : Rasheed got a playing top ($lattu$) as his
birthday present, which surprisingly had no colour on
it. He wanted to colour it with his crayons. The top is
shaped like a cone surmounted by a hemisphere
(see Fig 12.6). The entire top is 5 cm in height and
the diameter of the top is 3.5 cm. Find the area he
has to colour. (Take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ )

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : This top is exactly like the object we have discussed in Fig. 12.5. So, we
can conveniently use the result we have arrived at there. That is :

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: TSA of the toy = CSA of hemisphere + CSA of cone

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, the curved surface area of the hemisphere $= \frac{1}{2}(4\pi r^2) = 2\pi r^2$

$= \left( 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times \frac{3.5}{2} \times \frac{3.5}{2} \right) \text{cm}^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Also, the height of the cone = height of the top – height (radius) of the hemispherical part

$$= \left( 5 - \frac{3.5}{2} \right) \text{cm} = 3.25 \text{ cm}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, the slant height of the cone $(l) = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{\left(\frac{3.5}{2}\right)^2 + (3.25)^2}$ cm $= 3.7$ cm (approx.)

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, CSA of cone = $\pi rl = \left( \frac{22}{7} \times \frac{3.5}{2} \times 3.7 \right) \text{ cm}^2$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This gives the surface area of the top as

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$= \left( 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times \frac{3.5}{2} \times \frac{3.5}{2} \right) \text{cm}^2 + \left( \frac{22}{7} \times \frac{3.5}{2} \times 3.7 \right) \text{cm}^2$$

$$= \frac{22}{7} \times \frac{3.5}{2} (3.5 + 3.7) \text{ cm}^2 = \frac{11}{2} \times (3.5 + 3.7) \text{ cm}^2 = 39.6 \text{ cm}^2 \text{ (approx.)}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
You may note that ‘total surface area of the top’ is *not* the sum of the total
surface areas of the cone and hemisphere.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 2 : The decorative block shown
in Fig. 12.7 is made of two solids — a cube
and a hemisphere. The base of the block is a
cube with edge 5 cm, and the hemisphere
fixed on the top has a diameter of 4.2 cm.
Find the total surface area of the block.
(Take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Solution :** The total surface area of the cube $= 6 \times (\text{edge})^2 = 6 \times 5 \times 5 \text{ cm}^2 = 150 \text{ cm}^2$.
Note that the part of the cube where the hemisphere is attached is not included in the
surface area.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So, the surface area of the block = TSA of cube – base area of hemisphere
+ CSA of hemisphere
= $150 - \pi r^2 + 2 \pi r^2 = (150 + \pi r^2) \text{ cm}^2$
= $150 \text{ cm}^2 + \left( \frac{22}{7} \times \frac{4.2}{2} \times \frac{4.2}{2} \right) \text{ cm}^2$
= $(150 + 13.86) \text{ cm}^2 = 163.86 \text{ cm}^2$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Example 3 :** A wooden toy rocket is in the
shape of a cone mounted on a cylinder, as
shown in Fig. 12.8. The height of the entire
rocket is 26 cm, while the height of the conical
part is 6 cm. The base of the conical portion
has a diameter of 5 cm, while the base
diameter of the cylindrical portion is 3 cm. If
the conical portion is to be painted orange
and the cylindrical portion yellow, find the
area of the rocket painted with each of these
colours. (Take $\pi = 3.14$)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Solution :** Denote radius of cone by $r$, slant
height of cone by $l$, height of cone by $h$, radius
of cylinder by $r'$ and height of cylinder by $h'$.
Then $r = 2.5 \text{ cm}$, $h = 6 \text{ cm}$, $r' = 1.5 \text{ cm}$,
$h' = 26 - 6 = 20 \text{ cm}$ and

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Here, the conical portion has its circular base resting on the base of the cylinder, but
the base of the cone is larger than the base of the cylinder. So, a part of the base of the
cone (a ring) is to be painted.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So, the area to be painted orange = CSA of the cone + base area of the cone
- base area of the cylinder
$= \pi rl + \pi r^2 - \pi(r')^2$
$= \pi[(2.5 \times 6.5) + (2.5)^2 - (1.5)^2] \text{ cm}^2$
$= \pi[20.25] \text{ cm}^2 = 3.14 \times 20.25 \text{ cm}^2$
$= 63.585 \text{ cm}^2$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, the area to be painted yellow = CSA of the cylinder
+ area of one base of the cylinder
$= 2\pi r'h' + \pi(r')^2$
$= \pi r' (2h' + r')$
$= (3.14 \times 1.5) (2 \times 20 + 1.5) \text{ cm}^2$
$= 4.71 \times 41.5 \text{ cm}^2$
$= 195.465 \text{ cm}^2$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : Mayank made a bird-bath for his garden
in the shape of a cylinder with a hemispherical
depression at one end (see Fig. 12.9). The height of
the cylinder is 1.45 m and its radius is 30 cm. Find the
total surface area of the bird-bath. (Take $\pi = \frac{22}{7}$ )

Solution : Let $h$ be height of the cylinder, and $r$ the
common radius of the cylinder and hemisphere. Then,
the total surface area of the bird-bath = CSA of cylinder + CSA of hemisphere
$$= 2\pi rh + 2\pi r^2 = 2\pi r(h + r)$$
$$= 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 30(145 + 30) \text{ cm}^2$$
$$= 33000 \text{ cm}^2 = 3.3 \text{ m}^2$$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 12.3 Volume of a Combination of Solids

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous section, we have discussed how to find the surface area of solids made
up of a combination of two basic solids. Here, we shall see how to calculate their
volumes. It may be noted that in calculating the surface area, we have not added the
surface areas of the two constituents, because some part of the surface area disappeared
in the process of joining them. However, this will not be the case when we calculate
the volume. The volume of the solid formed by joining two basic solids will actually be
the sum of the volumes of the constituents, as we see in the examples below.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5 : Shanta runs an industry in
a shed which is in the shape of a cuboid
surmounted by a half cylinder (see Fig.
12.12). If the base of the shed is of

blocks.text:

blocks.text: So, the required volume = volume of the cuboid + $\frac{1}{2}$ volume of the cylinder

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the volume of the air, when there are machinery and workers

blocks.text:
Example 6 : A juice seller was serving his

blocks.label: Paragraph

blocks.text:
Example 7 : A solid toy is in the form of a

(Take $\pi = 3.14$)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Solution :** Let BPC be the hemisphere and ABC be the cone standing on the base
of the hemisphere (see Fig. 12.14). The radius BO of the hemisphere (as well as
of the cone) = $\frac{1}{2} \times 4 \text{ cm} = 2 \text{ cm}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So, volume of the toy = $\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3 + \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2h$
$= \left[ \frac{2}{3} \times 3.14 \times (2)^3 + \frac{1}{3} \times 3.14 \times (2)^2 \times 2 \right] \text{cm}^3 = 25.12 \text{ cm}^3$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let the right circular cylinder EFGH circumscribe the given solid. The radius of
the base of the right circular cylinder = HP = BO = 2 cm, and its height is

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$EH = AO + OP = (2 + 2) \text{ cm} = 4 \text{ cm}$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So, the volume required = volume of the right circular cylinder – volume of the toy
= $(3.14 \times 2^2 \times 4 - 25.12) \text{ cm}^3$
= $25.12 \text{ cm}^3$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Hence, the required difference of the two volumes $= 25.12 \text{ cm}^3$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 13.1 Introduction

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Class IX, you have studied the classification of given data into ungrouped as well as
grouped frequency distributions. You have also learnt to represent the data pictorially
in the form of various graphs such as bar graphs, histograms (including those of varying
widths) and frequency polygons. In fact, you went a step further by studying certain
numerical representatives of the ungrouped data, also called measures of central
tendency, namely, $mean$, $median$ and $mode$. In this chapter, we shall extend the study
of these three measures, i.e., mean, median and mode from ungrouped data to that of
$grouped$ $data$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 13.2 Mean of Grouped Data

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The mean (or average) of observations, as we know, is the sum of the values of all the
observations divided by the total number of observations. From Class IX, recall that if
$x_1, x_2, . . ., x_n$ are observations with respective frequencies $f_1, f_2, . . ., f_n$, then this
means observation $x_1$ occurs $f_1$ times, $x_2$ occurs $f_2$ times, and so on.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, the sum of the values of all the observations $= f_1x_1 + f_2x_2 + \dots + f_nx_n$, and
the number of observations $= f_1 + f_2 + \dots + f_n$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the mean $\bar{x}$ of the data is given by

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \bar{x} = \frac{f_1 x_1 + f_2 x_2 + \cdots + f_n x_n}{f_1 + f_2 + \cdots + f_n} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall that we can write this in short form by using the Greek letter $\Sigma$ (capital
sigma) which means summation. That is,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \bar{x} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i x_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} f_i} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
which, more briefly, is written as $\bar{x} = \frac{\sum f_i x_i}{\sum f_i}$ , if it is understood that $i$ varies from
1 to $n$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us apply this formula to find the mean in the following example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:

blocks.label: Paragraph

In most of our real life situations, data is usually so large that to make a meaningful
study it needs to be condensed as grouped data. So, we need to convert given ungrouped
data into grouped data and devise some method to find its mean.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us convert the ungrouped data of Example 1 into grouped data by forming
class-intervals of width, say 15. Remember that, while allocating frequencies to each
class-interval, students falling in any upper class-limit would be considered in the next
class, e.g., 4 students who have obtained 40 marks would be considered in the class-

lower limits. That is,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{Class mark} = \frac{\text{Upper class limit} + \text{Lower class limit}}{2} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph

We observe that Tables 13.1 and 13.3 are using the same data and employing the
same formula for the calculation of the mean but the results obtained are different.
Can you think why this is so, and which one is more accurate? The difference in the
two values is because of the mid-point assumption in Table 13.3, 59.3 being the exact

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Sometimes when the numerical values of $x_i$ and $f_i$ are large, finding the product
of $x_i$ and $f_i$ becomes tedious and time consuming. So, for such situations, let us think of
a method of reducing these calculations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We can do nothing with the $f_i$'s, but we can change each $x_i$ to a smaller number
so that our calculations become easy. How do we do this? What about subtracting a
fixed number from each of these $x_i$'s? Let us try this method.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The first step is to choose one among the $x_i$'s as the $assumed$ $mean$, and denote
it by '$a$'. Also, to further reduce our calculation work, we may take '$a$' to be that $x_i$
which lies in the centre of $x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$. So, we can choose $a = 47.5$ or $a = 62.5$. Let
us choose $a = 47.5$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The next step is to find the difference $d_i$ between $a$ and each of the $x_i$'s, that is,
the **deviation** of '$a$' from each of the $x_i$'s.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: STATISTICS

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The third step is to find the product of $d_i$ with the corresponding $f_i$, and take the sum
of all the $f_i d_i$'s. The calculations are shown in Table 13.4.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, from Table 13.4, the mean of the deviations, $\frac{\bar{d}}{d} = \frac{\Sigma f_i d_i}{\Sigma f_i}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, let us find the relation between $\bar{d}$ and $\bar{x}$.
Since in obtaining $d_i$, we subtracted '$a$' from each $x_i$, so, in order to get the mean
$\bar{x}$, we need to add '$a$' to $\bar{d}$. This can be explained mathematically as:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Mean of deviations, $\bar{d} = \frac{\Sigma f_i d_i}{\Sigma f_i}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
So,
$$ \begin{aligned} \bar{d} &= \frac{\Sigma f_i (x_i - a)}{\Sigma f_i} \\ &= \frac{\Sigma f_i x_i}{\Sigma f_i} - \frac{\Sigma f_i a}{\Sigma f_i} \\ &= \bar{x} - a \frac{\Sigma f_i}{\Sigma f_i} \\ &= \bar{x} - a \end{aligned} $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\bar{x} = a + \bar{d}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\bar{x} = a + \frac{\Sigma f_i d_i}{\Sigma f_i}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Substituting the values of $a$, $\Sigma f_i d_i$ and $\Sigma f_i$ from Table 13.4, we get

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the mean of the marks obtained by the students is 62.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The method discussed above is called the **Assumed Mean Method.**

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 1 : From the Table 13.3 find the mean by taking each of $x_i$ (i.e., 17.5, 32.5,
and so on) as ‘$a$’. What do you observe? You will find that the mean determined in
each case is the same, i.e., 62. (Why ?)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, we can say that the value of the mean obtained does not depend on the
choice of '$a$'.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Observe that in Table 13.4, the values in Column 4 are all multiples of 15. So, if
we divide the values in the entire Column 4 by 15, we would get smaller numbers to
multiply with $f_i$. (Here, 15 is the class size of each class interval.)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, let $u_i = \frac{x_i - a}{h}$, where $a$ is the assumed mean and $h$ is the class size.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now, we calculate $u_i$ in this way and continue as before (i.e., find $f_i u_i$ and
then $\Sigma f_i u_i$). Taking $h = 15$, let us form Table 13.5.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Let $\bar{u} = \frac{\Sigma f_i u_i}{\Sigma f_i}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Here, again let us find the relation between $\overline{u}$ and $\overline{x}$.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: STATISTICS

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: We have, $u_i = \frac{x_i - a}{h}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Therefore, $$\bar{u} = \frac{\Sigma f_i \frac{(x_i - a)}{h}}{\Sigma f_i} = \frac{1}{h} \left[ \frac{\Sigma f_i x_i - a \Sigma f_i}{\Sigma f_i} \right]$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ = \frac{1}{h} \left[ \frac{\Sigma f_i x_i}{\Sigma f_i} - a \frac{\Sigma f_i}{\Sigma f_i} \right] $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $h\overline{u} = \overline{x} - a$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: i.e., $\bar{x} = a + h\bar{u}$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: So, $\bar{x} = a + h \left( \frac{\sum f_i u_i}{\sum f_i} \right)$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, substituting the values of $a$, $h$, $\Sigma f_i u_i$ and $\Sigma f_i$ from Table 14.5, we get

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\bar{x} = 47.5 + 15 \times \left(\frac{29}{30}\right)$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the mean marks obtained by a student is 62.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The method discussed above is called the **Step-deviation** method.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We note that :

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ the step-deviation method will be convenient to apply if all the $d_i$'s have a
common factor.

$\bullet$ The mean obtained by all the three methods is the same.

$\bullet$ The assumed mean method and step-deviation method are just simplified
forms of the direct method.

$\bullet$ The formula $\bar{x} = a + h\bar{u}$ still holds if $a$ and $h$ are not as given above, but are

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: any non-zero numbers such that $u_i = \frac{x_i - a}{h}$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: 13.3 Mode of Grouped Data

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Recall from Class IX, a mode is that value among the observations which occurs most
often, that is, the value of the observation having the maximum frequency. Further, we
discussed finding the mode of ungrouped data. Here, we shall discuss ways of obtaining
a mode of grouped data. It is possible that more than one value may have the same
maximum frequency. In such situations, the data is said to be multimodal. Though
grouped data can also be multimodal, we shall restrict ourselves to problems having a
single mode only.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us first recall how we found the mode for ungrouped data through the following
example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 4 : The wickets taken by a bowler in 10 cricket matches are as follows:

$$2 \quad 6 \quad 4 \quad 5 \quad 0 \quad 2 \quad 1 \quad 3 \quad 2 \quad 3$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Find the mode of the data.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Let us form the frequency distribution table of the given data as follows:

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Number of
wickets		 0 1 2 3 4 5 6
Number of
matches		 1 1 3 2 1 1 1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Clearly, 2 is the number of wickets taken by the bowler in the maximum number
(i.e., 3) of matches. So, the mode of this data is 2.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In a grouped frequency distribution, it is not possible to determine the mode by
looking at the frequencies. Here, we can only locate a class with the maximum
frequency, called the **modal class**. The mode is a value inside the modal class, and is
given by the formula:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{Mode} = l + \left( \frac{f_1 - f_0}{2f_1 - f_0 - f_2} \right) \times h$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
where $l =$ lower limit of the modal class,
$h =$ size of the class interval (assuming all class sizes to be equal),
$f_1 =$ frequency of the modal class,
$f_0 =$ frequency of the class preceding the modal class,
$f_2 =$ frequency of the class succeeding the modal class.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us consider the following examples to illustrate the use of this formula.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 5 : A survey conducted on 20 households in a locality by a group of students
resulted in the following frequency table for the number of family members in a
household:

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Family size 1 - 3 3 - 5 5 - 7 7 - 9 9 - 11
Number of
families		 7 8 2 2 1

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Find the mode of this data.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Solution :** Here the maximum class frequency is $8$, and the class corresponding to this
frequency is $3 - 5$. So, the modal class is $3 - 5$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
modal class $= 3 - 5$, lower limit $(l)$ of modal class $= 3$, class size $(h) = 2$
frequency $(f_1)$ of the modal class $= 8$,
frequency $(f_0)$ of class preceding the modal class $= 7$,
frequency $(f_2)$ of class succeeding the modal class $= 2$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, let us substitute these values in the formula :

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: STATISTICS

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$\text{Mode} = l + \left( \frac{f_1 - f_0}{2f_1 - f_0 - f_2} \right) \times h$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Therefore, the mode of the data above is 3.286.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Example 6 : The marks distribution of 30 students in a mathematics examination are
given in Table 13.3 of Example 1. Find the mode of this data. Also compare and
interpret the mode and the mean.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:

(i.e., 7) have got marks in the interval 40 - 55, the modal class is 40 - 55. Therefore,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: the lower limit ( $l$ ) of the modal class $= 40$,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: the class size $(h) = 15,$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: the frequency ($f_1$) of modal class $= 7$,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: the frequency ($f_0$) of the class preceding the modal class $= 3$,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: the frequency ($f_2$) of the class succeeding the modal class $= 6$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, using the formula:

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Mode = $l + \left( \frac{f_1 - f_0}{2f_1 - f_0 - f_2} \right) \times h,$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: we get $\text{Mode} = 40 + \left( \frac{7 - 3}{14 - 6 - 3} \right) \times 15 = 52$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, the mode marks is 52.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now, from Example 1, you know that the mean marks is 62.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
So, the maximum number of students obtained 52 marks, while on an average a
student obtained 62 marks.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As you have studied in Class IX, the median is a measure of central tendency which
gives the value of the middle-most observation in the data. Recall that for finding the
median of ungrouped data, we first arrange the data values of the observations in

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: ascending order. Then, if $n$ is odd, the median is the $\left( \frac{n+1}{2} \right)$th observation. And, if $n$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: is even, then the median will be the average of the $\frac{n}{2}$ th and the $\left( \frac{n}{2} + 1 \right)$ th observations.
